title: What If You Woke Up 10 Years in the Past?
hook: I fell asleep at 24 and woke up at 14
description:
Jonah falls asleep at twenty-four and wakes up at fourteen, ten years in the past, with every memory of what happens next. He makes a list of four things to fix: his sister, his dad's bike shop, his best friend and an art contest he was too scared to enter. But fixing the future turns out to be the fastest way to miss the present. An original animated story about family, friendship and regret.

Facts in this story: Hermann Ebbinghaus's memory experiments in the 1880s produced the 'forgetting curve' (much new information fades within a day or two without review); the brain's prefrontal cortex keeps maturing until about the mid-twenties (US National Institute of Mental Health); and in a 1995 study, Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec found people regret actions more in the short run but inactions more in the long run.

#whatif #story #animation

scenes.say: Dad! I went to sleep twenty-four years old. Why am I fourteen?!
Because you are fourteen, Jonah. Get dressed. The first day of ninth grade waits for no one.
Last night I fell asleep in my tiny apartment. Twenty-four. A job, a car with a broken heater, and a sister who hadn't called me in years.
This morning I woke up in my old room. Dinosaur sheets. A calendar on the wall, exactly ten years in the past.
My name is Jonah. And somehow I'd been sent back ten years, with every memory of what happens next.
I walked into the kitchen like it was a museum. Everything I'd lost was just sitting there, making breakfast.
Why are you staring at me? Do I have toothpaste on my face or something?
My sister Tess. Sixteen. In my time, we only talked at holidays, and only about the weather.
And I knew exactly why. Because tonight, at nine fifteen, we have the worst fight of our lives.
I read her diary. She caught me. She said I wasn't her brother anymore. And for ten years, she kind of meant it.
Pancakes for the first day of school! It's not your birthday, but pancakes anyway.
That's Dad. Owner of Pedal and Patch, the tiny bike repair shop on Mill Street.
In my memory, that shop closes in two years. After that, Dad never really talks about it.
Looking at them was strange. It was like the future sat above their heads, glowing like a price tag.
So I grabbed a pen and made a list. Four things I would fix this time.
One, Tess. Two, Dad's shop. Three, Felix, my best friend, who moves away in March. I never said goodbye.
And four, the city art contest. The one I was too scared to enter.
Easy, right? I had ten years of answers. What could go wrong?
Everything. Everything could go wrong.
Jonah! Bro! Did you grow a mustache over the summer? No wait, that's just dirt.
Felix. My best friend since we were six. I hadn't heard that laugh in eight years. I almost cried right there in the hallway.
Are you crying? On the first day? Dude.
Allergies. Big allergies. I'm allergic to, uh, hallways.
Then math class started, and I discovered something terrible.
Ten years as an adult, and I'd forgotten everything about equations. My brain just showed a loading screen.
Turns out knowing the future doesn't make you smart. It just makes you nervous.
That night at nine o'clock, I sat on my bed and watched the clock like it was a bomb.
Tess's diary was on the hallway shelf. Exactly where I remembered. Purple cover, tiny gold lock.
The first time, I picked it up because I was bored and nosy. This time I didn't touch it. I just walked past.
Nine fifteen came. Nothing happened. No yelling. No slammed doors. Just the fridge humming.
I'd done it. I'd changed the future. Fix number one, done in a single night.
Night, weirdo.
Night, weirdo. Nicest thing she'd said to me in a decade. I fell asleep grinning.
Day four, I noticed something I didn't like at all.
I tried to remember my apartment. My job. My boss's name. And the details were blurry, like a dream after breakfast.
My memories of the future were fading. Fast.
There's a real thing called the forgetting curve. In the 1880s, a German scientist named Hermann Ebbinghaus tested his own memory, over and over.
He found that a lot of new information slips away within a day or two, unless you go over it again.
My future was new information to this brain. And this brain was throwing it out with the trash.
So I grabbed a notebook and wrote down everything I could still remember.
I called it the Future Book, and I hid it under my mattress like a pirate map.
The very first page said: Dad's shop. Fix it before it's too late.
Pedal and Patch smelled like rubber, oil and Dad's terrible coffee. I loved that smell more than anything.
Hand me the tire lever, kiddo. No, the blue one. The other blue one.
In my memory, a giant sports store opened across town, and nobody needed a tiny repair shop anymore.
But I knew something Dad didn't. In a few years, everybody in town would ride electric bikes and scooters.
Dad. You need to start fixing electric bikes. And scooters. Like, now. Trust me.
Electric bikes? Those cost more than my truck. Who's going to buy those around here?
Everybody. In three years, everybody.
Oh, in three years. Okay, fortune teller. What are next week's lottery numbers?
I didn't know any lottery numbers. Nobody remembers lottery numbers. That's the first thing time travel teaches you.
But I pushed. Every day. I even printed a business plan on the school printer.
Twelve pages. With graphs. I was very proud of the graphs.
Jonah, where is this coming from? Do you think the shop is failing?
And I said the worst possible thing. I said, I know it is.
He didn't yell. Dad never yelled. He just went very quiet, folded the plan and put it in his apron pocket.
Okay. Thanks for the homework, bud. Go on home. I'll close up.
I walked home feeling like I'd fixed something. I had no idea I had just broken something else.
Week two. Felix wanted to hang out every day. Skate park, video games, gas station slushies.
Saturday, skate park? I finally learned the drop-in. Kind of. I fall like forty percent of the time.
Can't. I've got, uh, stuff.
The stuff was the Future Book. Every afternoon I wrote down memories before they disappeared.
You've had stuff every day for two weeks, man.
I told myself it was fine. Felix moves in March. I had months. I'd hang out with him later, after I fixed everything important.
Later. That word is going to come back. Remember it.
Meanwhile, things with Tess were polite. Too polite.
No fight. No diary. But no real talking either. She'd go straight to her room and close the door softly.
In my first life, I blamed the diary. Now there was no diary, and she was still behind that door.
So the fight was never the reason. The fight was just the moment I finally noticed.
One night I heard something through the wall. Very quiet. Tess was crying.
Fourteen-year-old me would've put on headphones. Twenty-four-year-old me knocked.
Go away, Jonah. I'm fine.
I'm fine. I'd said those words a thousand times as an adult. I knew exactly what they meant.
I'm not going away. I'll just sit here. You don't have to say anything.
I sat on the hallway floor for twenty minutes. My legs fell asleep. Then the door opened, just a little.
Dad's shop is in trouble. I heard him on the phone with the bank. He's been working nights. I didn't want to scare you.
She'd been carrying it alone. For months. That was what the diary was about the first time. Not boys or friends. Us.
I'd been so busy fixing the future, I never asked what my family was carrying right now.
And then came the big problem. The kind no notebook can fix.
Dad took my business plan seriously. Way too seriously.
He took out a loan, bought a whole wall of electric bike parts, and stayed late every night teaching himself to fix them.
Three years too early. Nobody in town was buying electric bikes yet. Not one customer came in.
The parts just sat there in boxes, stacked to the ceiling. And Dad's face got more tired every week.
In my first life, the shop closed in two years. In this version, I'd made it worse. It might not last until spring.
I'd forgotten something important about the future. Being right too early can look exactly like being wrong.
And it got worse. Dad started missing dinner. Then he missed Tess's swim meet, the one she'd trained for all year.
He said he'd come. He promised.
In my first life, Dad was at that meet. Front row, holding a sign with her name spelled wrong. I remembered that sign.
This time the seat was empty. Because of me.
I opened the Future Book and stared at it. Forty pages of answers, and not one of them helped.
Real fact: the part of your brain behind your forehead, the part that plans and controls impulses, keeps developing until about your mid-twenties.
I had a twenty-four-year-old's memories, but a fourteen-year-old's brain. And honestly? It showed.
And in the middle of all that, Felix showed up at my door holding a skateboard and a cardboard box.
So. My dad got the new job early. We're moving. Saturday.
Saturday. Not March. Saturday. Four days away.
Maybe my changes had rippled out somehow. Maybe I'd just remembered it wrong. Either way, my later had just turned into now.
I wanted to tell you sooner. But you've been kind of gone. Like you're here, but you're not here.
You act like you're forty, man. Where'd my friend go?
I didn't have an answer. Because he was right. I'd been living in a future that didn't exist yet.
And I was missing the one friend who was standing right in front of me.
Saturday was going to be a disaster. Everything I cared about, on the same day.
Ten a.m., Felix's moving truck leaves. Noon, the art contest closes. And Dad had planned one big repair day at the shop to bring customers in.
So on Friday night, I did something I'd never done in either life. I asked for help.
Tess. I messed up. With Dad, with the shop, with everything. I can't fix it alone.
And my sister, the one who stopped calling me in my other life, put down her phone.
Okay. So we don't fix it alone. What do we have?
Turns out we had a lot. Tess had her whole swim team group chat. I had a sketchbook.
And Dad had a whole wall of electric bike parts that nobody wanted. Yet.
We stayed up until two a.m. making posters. Free bike checkups. Kids ride free.
I drew them. Tess wrote the words. For the first time in ten years, we laughed at the same joke.
At six a.m., we taped them to every pole on Mill Street.
At nine, I ran to Felix's house. Not with a plan. Not with a speech. Just running.
The moving truck was already half full. Felix was sitting on the curb, holding his skateboard.
Hey. You said you learned the drop-in?
Kind of. Forty percent falling, remember?
So we went to the skate park. One last hour. He fell. I fell. We fell a lot.
It was the best hour of my whole life. And I've had two lives.
Before he left, I gave him a drawing. Us at six, wearing cooking pots as helmets. No Future Book needed for that one.
You're weird, man. Call me, okay? Like, actually call me.
In my first life, I never called. This time I wrote his number on my hand. In pen. Twice.
Eleven forty. The art contest closed at noon. And I had nothing to submit.
Wait. Not nothing. I'd snapped a photo of that drawing of Felix and me before I gave it away.
I could have drawn something amazing with my grown-up skills. But it wouldn't have been honest. It wouldn't have been fourteen-year-old Jonah.
So I submitted the skate park drawing. Messy. Real. Mine. At eleven fifty-eight.
Then I ran to the shop, and I stopped dead in the middle of the street.
There was a line. An actual line. Kids with flat tires. Grandparents with rusty bikes. Tess's whole swim team, holding up our posters.
And one guy with an electric bike nobody else in town knew how to fix.
Jonah! Grab the blue tire lever! No, the other blue one!
We fixed thirty-one bikes that day. Dad didn't stop smiling once.
At five o'clock, he sat down on an upside-down bucket and looked at the two of us.
Tess, I'm sorry I missed your meet. And Jonah, I'm sorry I made your plan my whole life.
I was so scared of losing the shop, I forgot what the shop was for.
What's it for?
This. You two, arguing over a tire lever.
And I realized he wasn't talking about bikes at all.
The shop didn't get saved that day. One good Saturday doesn't pay off a loan. But something else did.
That night I fell asleep on the couch, Felix's number on my hand. My future memory was almost gone.
And then I woke up. Twenty-four again. My tiny apartment. Broken heater. Same ceiling.
For a second I thought it was all a dream. Then my phone buzzed.
Three messages. The first from Tess. Sunday dinner at Dad's? You're bringing dessert. No store-bought.
The second from Felix. A video of him, still falling off a skateboard ten years later. Caption: forty percent.
And the third, a photo from Dad. The shop. Not on Mill Street anymore. Smaller. But open.
In the window, a hand-painted sign. Electric Bikes Welcome. Kids Ride Free. In letters I knew, because I drew them.
Some things I couldn't change. The shop still moved. My heater is still broken.
And I didn't win the art contest. Third place, and a coupon for free pizza.
But here's something real. In a well-known 1995 study, psychologists Thomas Gilovich and Victoria Medvec looked at what people regret.
In the short run, people mostly regret things they did. But looking back over many years, they regret the things they didn't do.
I didn't need to fix the future. I needed to stop missing the present.
Knock on the door. Go to the skate park. Ask for help.
You probably won't wake up ten years in the past. Nobody gets that. But you have today.
So here's my question. If you woke up ten years ago tomorrow, what's the first thing you'd fix? Tell me in the comments.
And then maybe go do it today. Me? I'm going to call Felix. Like, actually call him.

shorts.top: I tried to fix the future. I made it WORSE
shorts.title: I Used the Future to Help My Dad. Big Mistake.
